history: Saldo, soldi and saldare are one family. Latin solidus meant ‘solid, firm’, and as a noun it named a gold coin of the late Roman Empire. The coin passed into Italian as soldo, a small coin, and the plural soldi became the everyday word for money. The adjective gave the verb saldare, ‘to make firm’, so ‘to weld’ and also ‘to settle a debt’, as if you closed the account. From it comes il saldo, the balance of an account: saldo del conto. The same word is used for sales. I saldi are the seasonal sales, when the remaining stock is cleared. The adjective saldo still means ‘firm’.
historyEinfach: Saldo, soldi and saldare come from Latin solidus, ‘firm, solid’. Solidus was also the name of a gold coin. In Italian, soldi means ‘money’. Saldare means ‘to weld’ and ‘to pay a debt completely’. Il saldo is the balance of your account. I saldi are the sales in the shops.
